bug-reports.starter:
# Bug triage engine: classify a failing test as REAL DEFECT or FLAKE,
# then assign severity + CI gate action, following the lesson's logic.
#
# Rule the lesson taught (BUG-1471 checkout race):
#   - A failure that is DETERMINISTIC in CI (same result every CI run) and
#     traces to a code-level race/order bug is a REAL DEFECT, not a flake.
#   - A failure that is INTERMITTENT across identical runs (passes sometimes,
#     fails sometimes with no code change) is a FLAKE.
#   - REAL DEFECT on the primary revenue flow => Severity S1 => gate RED (hold release).
#   - REAL DEFECT off the revenue flow      => Severity S2 => gate RED.
#   - FLAKE => quarantine the test => Severity S4 => gate GREEN (do not hold release).

# Each report: (bug_id, ci_results, blocks_revenue_flow, root_cause_is_code)
#   ci_results: list of "pass"/"fail" from repeated IDENTICAL CI runs (no code change)
REPORTS = [
    ("BUG-1471", ["fail", "fail", "fail", "fail", "fail"], True,  True),
    ("BUG-2033", ["pass", "fail", "pass", "fail", "pass"], False, False),
    ("BUG-3100", ["fail", "fail", "fail"],                 False, True),
]

def is_deterministic(ci_results):
    return len(set(ci_results)) == 1

def triage(ci_results, blocks_revenue_flow, root_cause_is_code):
    always_fails = is_deterministic(ci_results) and ci_results[0] == "fail"
    if always_fails and root_cause_is_code:
        verdict = "REAL_DEFECT"
        severity = "S1" if blocks_revenue_flow else "S2"
        gate = "RED"
    else:
        verdict = "FLAKE"
        severity = "S4"
        gate = "GREEN"
    return verdict, severity, gate

# TODO: iterate REPORTS, triage each one, and print one line per report as:
#   "<bug_id> <VERDICT> <SEVERITY> gate=<GATE>"
#   e.g.  BUG-1471 REAL_DEFECT S1 gate=RED
# Track whether ANY gate is RED. After the loop, print:
#   "HOLD_RELEASE: <True/False>"
# (True if any gate is RED, otherwise False)

# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.
# Retain one minimized failing case as a regression and name the production evidence still required.
bug-reports.check:
BUG-1471 REAL_DEFECT S1 gate=RED
BUG-2033 FLAKE S4 gate=GREEN
BUG-3100 REAL_DEFECT S2 gate=RED
HOLD_RELEASE: True

release-risk-scoring.text: It is release night on the checkout flow. Two Playwright specs are red — but they were red yesterday too, and green the run before that. The VP asks the one question that decides revenue: 'Is that a real bug, or is the test lying?' The room that can score the difference ships; the room that can't either blocks good code or leaks a real defect to production.

A red test is not the same as a shipping decision — a flaky spec and a genuine regression both show up red. Release risk scoring converts a wall of raw pass/fail signal into one defensible gate call, backed by the trace, contract, and a11y evidence a reviewer can replay.

release-risk-scoring.prompt: Two specs fail in CI but pass on your laptop. Same commit. Before you touch anything — is that a safer release or a riskier one than two specs failing everywhere? Decide before reading on.
release-risk-scoring.reveal: Riskier — because 'passes locally, fails in CI' is the exact signature of weak assumptions: race-prone locators, timing waits, unseeded fixtures, environment drift. A failure that reproduces everywhere is at least honest; you can diagnose it. A failure that only appears in CI hides which side is lying — the test or the code — so your risk score has to account for detectability, not just whether it's red. The dangerous release isn't the one with red tests; it's the one where you can't tell flaky from broken.

# SDET Quality Gate & Flake Repair Packet — checkout release
Context: revenue-critical checkout flow; release blocked by 2 red specs + 3 a11y defects.

## Risk scores (severity 1-5 × likelihood 1-5 × detectability 1-5 = score)
| Axis            | Sev | Lik | Det | Score | Evidence hook                                  |
|-----------------|-----|-----|-----|-------|------------------------------------------------|
| Flaky specs     |  2  |  4  |  2  |  16   | npx playwright test --trace=on -> show-report  |
| Contract drift  |  5  |  2  |  4  |  40   | POST /api/checkout schema snapshot diff        |
| A11y defects    |  4  |  5  |  3  |  60   | axe scan: cart total has no accessible name    |

## Triage (flaky axis): trace stable across retries, only a 500ms timing wait failed
-> classify as FLAKE, quarantine spec `checkout.spec.ts:payButton`, file repair ticket

## Selected gate: CONDITIONAL-SHIP
- Rejected: hard BLOCK on all red (would block on a proven flake -> false confidence cost)
- Condition to flip to HOLD: any a11y defect on the pay button itself (blocks screen readers from paying)

## Invalidation: score is void if the flaky trace later reproduces a real state change
## CI gate result: quarantined flake = amber, a11y P1 = red until fixed -> gate HOLDS on a11y
steps: Predict the release decision before executing.
Score three axes, not one: Severity × likelihood × detectability — the third factor is what beginners drop. A low-detectability risk (you can't easily see it) is scarier at the same severity.
The flaky-spec row: High likelihood, LOW detectability (2) — you often can't tell flaky from broken. That low score of 16 is honest only because the trace resolved it.
The contract-drift row: Severity 5: a checkout schema break loses money silently. High score even at low likelihood — severity dominates when the failure is invisible to users until it's too late.
Every score cites a hook: No number without `--trace=on`, a schema diff, or an axe scan behind it. This column is what makes the score replayable instead of asserted.
Triage the flake, don't just block: Replay the trace across retries. Stable trace + a lone timing wait = flake → quarantine it. A test that can only ever say 'red' teaches the gate nothing.

The gate + the rejected option + the flip condition: Conditional-ship, NOT block-on-all-red (that penalizes proven flakes). Name what would move it to HOLD — here, an a11y defect on the pay button itself.
Change one risk, boundary, timing, environment, or assertion and identify the evidence needed to prevent a false pass.

storyboard.say: It's release night on checkout. A CI run finishes and emits raw pass/fail signal — two Playwright specs are red again.
That wall of red isn't a decision. We fan the raw signal out per axis so each risk gets scored on its own evidence.
For every axis we score severity times likelihood times detectability — from a replayable trace, contract check, or a11y result, never gut feel.
The flaky-spec axis is the hard one, so it branches into triage: is the test lying, or is it catching a real bug?
If the trace is stable and only timing wobbled, it's a real flake — quarantine it so it can't hold the release hostage.
If the trace shows a genuine defect, we block — a red that means revenue is at risk raises the bar to ship.
Every path converges on one gate: contained flakes and clean a11y-plus-contract axes let it pass; a real block stops it.
The insight: the gate follows the scores, and every number traces to a trace, a contract, or an a11y result a reviewer can replay.

release-risk-scoring.question: Your risk packet says the flaky-spec axis scores low. The review board pushes back: 'Prove that's a flake and not a real regression you're waving through.' What is the exact evidence that answers them?
options: The spec passed on your laptop three times in a row, so it's clearly the CI environment.
A Playwright trace replayed across retries shows a stable DOM/state — only a timing wait failed — so the code path is unchanged; you quarantine the spec and file a repair ticket.
You re-ran the whole suite and it went green this time.
The spec has failed intermittently for weeks, so everyone already agrees it's flaky.
release-risk-scoring.explanation: Only option 2 is replayable evidence a reviewer can inspect: the trace shows the application state was identical across retries and only a timing assertion flaked — that distinguishes a flake from a masked regression. 'Passed on my laptop' (1) is the exact failure signature you're supposed to distrust; a lucky green re-run (3) proves nothing; and 'everyone agrees' (4) is social proof, not a trace.

quality-review-board.doNotClaim: Do not claim a Quality Review Board 'approved the release' if the packet only describes quality in the abstract. A gate with no replayable flake evidence and no accessibility result is a rubber stamp, not a review. The board owns the decision and the proof, not a vibe that 'tests looked green'.

quality-review-board.text: Friday, 4 p.m., a revenue-critical checkout flow is one merge from release — but three browser tests failed twice and passed once, and two accessibility defects sit untriaged. The room wants a thumbs-up; the Quality Review Board asks the only question that matters: 'Is this flakiness or a real regression, and can a keyboard user still check out?'

A Quality Review Board is where an SDET converts product risk into an inspectable release decision — separating flake from regression, triaging conformance defects, and gating on evidence a reviewer can replay. It sits at the end of SDET Operations: the last checkpoint before revenue-critical code ships.

quality-review-board.prompt: A checkout test failed in CI but passes when you re-run it locally. The board is asked to sign off because 'it's just flaky.' What is wrong with shipping on that reasoning? Answer before reading on.
quality-review-board.reveal: 'Just flaky' is an untriaged verdict wearing a decision's clothes. Local pass proves nothing — CI differs in timing, viewport, network, and fixture state, which is exactly where checkout regressions hide. The board's job is to open the Playwright trace, watch the failed step, and prove it was a timing/selector flake and NOT a real broken 'Place order' button. Calling it flake without the trace is how a revenue regression ships behind a green-looking dashboard.

quality-review-board.setup: Convene a Quality Review Board for a real (or realistic) release blocked by flaky browser tests and untriaged accessibility defects. Produce a signed release-gate decision packet: the constraint, the ship/hold call, the rejected option, the flake and a11y evidence, and the reversal condition — all inspectable by another reviewer.
quality-review-board.code:
# 1. Reproduce the exact CI failure locally, WITH a trace on every run
npx playwright test checkout.spec.ts \
  --project=chromium \
  --retries=0 \
  --repeat-each=5 \
  --trace=on

# 2. Open the trace for the failed attempt — watch the step that broke
npx playwright show-report

# Trace reading (what the board records in the packet):
#   step: getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).click()
#   -> attempt 3/5 FAILED: element detached during re-render, click lost
#   -> attempts 1,2,4,5 PASSED: same selector, same assertion
#   VERDICT: FLAKE (race on re-render), NOT a broken checkout button

# 3. Repair the flake at the root: web-first assertion waits for actionability
#   BEFORE: await page.locator('.btn-primary').click()          // brittle
#   AFTER:  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' })
#             .click()                                            // auto-waits

# 4. Prove the repair holds AND accessibility still passes the gate
npx playwright test checkout.spec.ts --repeat-each=10 --trace=on   # 10/10 green
npx playwright test a11y.spec.ts --grep @axe                       # keyboard + contrast
steps: Predict the release decision before executing.

Reproduce under trace, not vibes: --repeat-each=5 --retries=0 forces the intermittent failure to surface; --trace=on captures the DOM, network, and each action so the board can watch what actually broke.
Open the report and trace: The trace viewer is the board's evidence exhibit. You do not argue 'it's flaky' — you point at the failed step and its screenshot timeline.

Read the trace: flake or regression: Same selector, same assertion, mixed pass/fail on a re-render race = flake. If ALL attempts failed on a missing button, that is a real checkout regression — HOLD the release.

Repair at the root, not with a sleep: A role-based locator with a web-first assertion auto-waits for actionability. Adding a fixed timeout would hide the flake, not kill it — the board rejects that repair.
Prove the repair and re-check a11y: 10/10 green under repeat proves the flake is dead; the axe run proves the keyboard/contrast defects the board flagged are actually cleared before ship.
Change one risk, boundary, timing, environment, or assertion and identify the evidence needed to prevent a false pass.

storyboard.say: Friday, 4 p.m.: a revenue-critical checkout flow arrives as a release candidate and submits itself to the CI quality gate.
The gate fans the candidate into three evidence streams — flake triage, accessibility, and contract — because a green light alone proves nothing.
Three browser tests failed twice and passed once; CI hands the failing spec and its trace to flake triage.
This is the suspect edge: a flaky test can fake a false-green gate, so the board asks — flakiness or a real regression?
In parallel, two untriaged accessibility defects get a severity, and the contract proof returns a hard pass or fail.
The board converts all three streams into one verdict: ship, hold, or fix — backed by evidence any reviewer can replay.
Only on that evidence does code reach the revenue flow — the invariant holds: no evidence, no gate.

quality-review-board.text: The senior tell in a review board is triage discipline: not every accessibility defect blocks a release, and not every red test is a regression. A blocker (keyboard user cannot complete checkout) holds the ship; a lower-severity defect (a decorative-image alt-text gap) ships with a filed ticket. A board that treats all defects as equal blocks forever; a board that treats them all as ignorable ships broken. The skill is the severity call — and defending it with evidence.

quality-review-board.question: The board is shown a checkout test that failed once in CI and passed on re-run. What is the minimum evidence required before recording a 'flake, safe to ship' verdict?
options: The engineer's statement that it passes locally now.

A Playwright trace of the failed run showing mixed pass/fail on the identical selector/assertion (a race), plus a repeat-each re-run that is green — proving the failure was non-deterministic, not a real regression.
A green CI dashboard on the latest run.
A comment in the PR saying 'known flaky, ignore.'
quality-review-board.explanation: Flake and regression look identical on a dashboard — the difference is only visible in the trace. A local pass (1), a single green run (3), or a hand-wave comment (4) cannot distinguish a timing race from a genuinely broken 'Place order' button. Only the trace showing an identical selector passing and failing non-deterministically, backed by a repeat-each green run, lets the board honestly certify flake rather than smuggle a revenue regression past the gate.

quality-review-board.starter:
# Quality Review Board: flake vs. real-bug verdict
#
# When a test fails in CI, the board reruns it with --repeat-each and reads the
# trace of EVERY attempt before ruling. A test that fails on some attempts but
# passes on others is a FLAKE (a race, e.g. an element detaching during
# re-render) -- NOT a broken feature. A test that fails on every single attempt
# is genuinely BROKEN. A test that passes every attempt is STABLE.
#
# The packet below is the CI evidence: each test maps to its per-attempt
# results from `playwright test --repeat-each=5 --trace=on`.
#
# The board's rule:
#   - EVERY attempt "PASS"        -> "STABLE"
#   - EVERY attempt "FAIL"        -> "BROKEN"
#   - a MIX of "PASS" and "FAIL"  -> "FLAKE"
#
# Print one line per test, sorted by test name (ascending), formatted as:
#   <test_name>: <VERDICT> (<passed>/<total> passed)

packet = {
    "checkout.spec.ts":  ["PASS", "PASS", "FAIL", "PASS", "PASS"],
    "login.spec.ts":     ["PASS", "PASS", "PASS", "PASS", "PASS"],
    "search.spec.ts":    ["FAIL", "FAIL", "FAIL", "FAIL", "FAIL"],
    "cart.spec.ts":      ["FAIL", "PASS", "FAIL", "PASS", "PASS"],
}


def verdict(results):
    # TODO: return a tuple (label, passed, total) where:
    #   - passed = number of "PASS" attempts
    #   - total  = number of attempts
    #   - label  = "STABLE" if all passed, "BROKEN" if none passed,
    #              otherwise "FLAKE"
    pass


# TODO: for each test name in sorted order, compute the verdict and print:
#   f"{name}: {label} ({passed}/{total} passed)"

# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.
# Retain one minimized failing case as a regression and name the production evidence still required.

quality-review-board.intro: Prove your Quality Review Board gate holds — no rubber stamp:
items: Your packet contains a Playwright trace reference for every 'flake' verdict, showing mixed pass/fail on an identical selector — not just a re-run that happened to pass.
Every accessibility defect has a triaged severity (blocker vs ship-with-ticket) that you can defend, not a blanket 'defer'.
The CI gate decision is recorded with the concrete run IDs: the failing run and the green run that proves the repair.
One rejected option is written down with the constraint it violates (e.g. 'ship-and-hotfix' violates the no-broken-revenue-flow constraint).
A reversal condition is stated — the exact evidence that would flip ship back to hold (e.g. repeat-each drops below 10/10, or a11y blocker reopens).

prompts: In your own words: why can a board never certify 'flake' from a dashboard alone, and what does the trace add that the dashboard cannot?
Explain your severity call on one accessibility defect — why it was a blocker or ship-with-ticket — using your own packet as the example.
What is the one constraint your board refused to violate, and which tempting option (ship-and-hotfix, ignore-the-defect) did it eliminate?
